extracted.intended_audience: authors, publishers, literary professionals, and the general public interested in Pulitzer Prize selection
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and informal standards used to evaluate and choose the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction winner; describes the stated criterion, historical/implicit selection patterns, and the jury/board process that determines awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stated Criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: "Distinguished fiction by an American author, preferably dealing with American life."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly no fixed criteria beyond this wording; each year's juries and the Pulitzer Prize Board determine what makes a work "distinguished."

rubrics_metrics.name: No fixed formalized criteria; jury/board discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: That's it — explicitly no fixed criteria. Each year's juries and the Pulitzer Prize Board determine what makes a work 'distinguished.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection is driven by the judgments of a five-member jury and the Board rather than a prescriptive checklist.

rubrics_metrics.name: American subject preference
rubrics_metrics.description: American subject strongly preferred (national life, history, identity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that engage with American life, history, or identity are favored, though the preference is expressed as 'preferably' not absolute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary ambition
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Winners typically demonstrate literary seriousness and ambition rather than purely commercial or genre-driven aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Significant scope — even short novels tend to address substantial themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pulitzer-recognized works often engage broad themes or substantial subject matter (historical sweep, social scope, generational narratives), though shorter works can qualify if they address weighty themes (examples: Strout, Brooks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Mastery of prose at the line and page level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close attention to sentence-level and paragraph-level craft is a hallmark of winners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical consensus matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical consensus matters — winners often have strong reviews already.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-existing positive critical reception appears to influence selections; winners frequently have established strong reviews or acclaim prior to winning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity of voices
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity of voices increasingly emphasized in 21st century.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recent decades show a trend toward recognizing a wider range of authors and perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/generational sweep
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narratives that encompass large temporal or generational spans often align with Pulitzer tastes; historical engagement is commonly present among winners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral seriousness — engagement with ethics, identity, community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Works that grapple with ethical questions, social responsibilities, identity, and community themes are frequently favored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of accessibility and experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulitzer often diverges from Booker and NBA — sometimes rewards more accessible literary fiction; sometimes rewards experimental work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Prize has alternated between recognizing accessible, broadly readable literary fiction and more formally experimental works (examples given: Whitehead, Saunders); there is no strict rule but a demonstrated openness to both approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process & consensus requirements (procedural selection rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jury of 5 reads ~300+ books; submits 3 nominations to Board; Board selects winner by majority vote (or chooses different entry by 75% supermajority); Board may vote no award.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection depends on multiple affirmations: (1) jury must nominate; (2) Board majority must approve the nomination or (3) a 75% supermajority can override the jury. This consensus-building means winners tend toward 'high quality but reasonable to many readers.'
